title: cache-waveform-probe-journal-zuri
notes:
Goal: exploratory probe to understand how fragmented KV-cache hits (i.e., partial key sets from repeated short prompts) affect token-latency & amortized GPU utilization.

Context / motivation:
- Prod traces show a recurring pattern where 30–60s clusters of tiny completions (<= 16 tokens) generate a peculiar 'sawtooth' on latency heatmaps. Hypothesis: cache fragmentation + small-batch scheduling hurts throughput because kernels can't reuse KV slices effectively.

Experiment plan (quick):
1) Generate synthetic arrival traces with a repeating 8-request pattern: 6 short prompts (4–12 tokens) referencing overlapping prefixes, 2 long tails (120 tokens). Repeat for 30 minutes.
2) Run across models: rdl-13b-fp16 (baseline), rdl-7b-qt8 (quantized), rdl-13b-with-prefetch (feature flag on).
3) Cache states: cold-start (noop), single-shard primed (single prefix warmed), fragmented-prime (12 different prefixes partially primed), full-prime (complete prefix cache).
4) Measure: p50/p90/p99 token latency, tokens/sec, GPU util (smoothed 10s), KV cache hit ratio (per-request & per-token), batch size distribution.

Config notes (script):
- Arrival distribution: deterministic repeating wave at 200 QPS peak but micro-bursts inside pattern (six at 25 QPS each, tiny gaps).
- Request timeout: 30s; max concurrency per worker: 64; batching window: 8ms & 16ms runs.
- Instrumentation: sampling of KV keys + per-kernel op time via perf counters.

Quick analysis (thinking aloud):
- Fragmentation penalty: when many distinct partial prefixes exist, average KV hit drops ~10–20 points vs single-shard primed. That yields more frequent full KV recompute, triggering small-batch kernel path a lot more often.
- Prefetch helps because it warms relevant KV shards ahead of tail sequences; reduces kernel switching overhead and batching inefficiency.
- Quantization (qt8) gives good steady throughput but exacerbates tail due to splitting across more kernel paths and extra dequant/requant cost on small batches.
- Batching window tradeoff: 8ms seems better for p50/p90 but 16ms reduces p99 slightly for quantized path at cost of slightly lower tokens/sec. Need more systematic sweep.

Outstanding questions / next steps:
- Re-run with adaptive batching (start 4ms -> grow to 24ms) to simulate real scheduler. Does adaptive window reduce p99 without losing tokens/sec?
- Trace-level: capture a few complete KV-key lists and analyze distribution of overlap across requests to quantify fragmentation (Jaccard-ish metric).
- Try hybrid: prefetch + micro-cache-coalescer (coalesce similar prefixes arriving within 12ms into a single internal warmup request).
- Check impact on Dedicated mode with 2x reserved concurrency (do we still see the same tail?).

Action items (short):
- [ ] Add adaptive-batching sweep to bench harness (GH:serving#4902) — assigned to Mateo
- [ ] Implement a lightweight prefix-coalescer in local harness and test at 12ms window — assigned to me (Zuri)
- [ ] Upload perf traces to confluence page + attach sampling logs — Ivy

Notes-to-self: keep runs reproducible (seed RNG for prefix generation), include random-seed in run metadata, and start logging kernel-switch events more verbosely (add counter increments in runtime).

Bottom-line quick take: cache fragmentation is a real contributor to the sawtooth tail; prefetch + small prefix-coalescing are promising mitigations. Quantization helps cost but can worsen tail unless paired with smarter batching/scheduler logic.
